title: Price in your own stumbles
allegory: SARSA is a hiker who knows she stumbles one step in ten: she rates each move by the step she actually took next, slip included, so the ground beside a cliff earns a bad reputation and she learns a safer path away from the edge.
map: the spot you stand on and the step you choose
the state s and the action a
one step in ten is a random stumble
rating a step by the step you actually took next, slip included
the SARSA target r + γ·Q(s′, a′), with a′ the action really taken
the optimist who rates by his best possible next step

cap.1: Walk from one corner of a grid to the other. The bottom edge is a cliff: step off, lose 100 points, start again. The short way runs right along the edge.
cap.2: CliffWalking-v0: every step costs 1 point, falling costs 100. The shortest path hugs the cliff; a safer one keeps its distance and takes a few more steps. Which does an agent learn?
cap.3: Sutton and Barto's Example 6.6 as gymnasium's CliffWalking-v0, trained with γ = 1, ε = 0.1, lr = 0.1 and no optimistic initialisation.

cap.1: Now the hiker stumbles one step in ten. If she rates each move by the step she actually takes next, stumbles included, the cliff edge earns a bad reputation.
cap.2: SARSA learns from the action it actually takes next, chosen by its own ε-greedy policy. When a random step tips it off the edge, that −100 flows back into the value of standing near the edge.
cap.3: SARSA's target samples the behaviour policy at s′, so its fixed point is Q_π for the ε-greedy π, not Q*. The exploration's cliff risk is priced into the edge-adjacent states.

parts.note: the step you really took next

cap.1: The update uses five things: where you stood, what you did, what you got, where you landed, and what you did next. That's where the name comes from.
cap.2: Nudge Q(s, a) towards r + γ·Q(s′, a′), where a′ is the action the agent really takes next. State, action, reward, state, action: S-A-R-S-A.
cap.3: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γQ(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)]: on-policy TD(0) control. Rummery and Niranjan proposed it in 1994 as 'modified Q-learning'; Sutton later renamed it SARSA.

chapters.name: Safe or short?

left.title: SARSA
lines: rates by the step actually taken

right.title: Q-learning
lines: rates by the best next step

chapters.verdict: Which is better depends on whether you'll still be stumbling when it counts.

cap.1: The optimist rates each move by his best next step, so he hugs the edge and keeps falling off while learning. Without stumbles, though, his route is shorter.
cap.2: Q-learning bootstraps off max Q(s′, ·) and learns the cliff-edge path; SARSA learns the detour. During training SARSA earns more; greedy rollouts give Q-learning about −13 and SARSA about −17.
cap.3: SARSA optimises the policy you will run, exploration included; Q-learning optimises the one you would run if you stopped exploring. Online return favours SARSA, greedy return favours Q-learning.

cap.1: The easiest way to break SARSA: decide your next step twice, once for the rating and once for the walk. Then the stumbles never reach the rating.
cap.2: If you compute a′ with an argmax inside the update, or sample a fresh action when you step the env, the random branch vanishes from the update. You've written Q-learning with extra bookkeeping.
cap.3: Thread one sampled a′ into both the TD target and the next env.step. Test it: train both at ε = 0.1, roll out greedily; SARSA near −17, Q-learning near −13. Equal numbers mean the bug.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: On-policy: learn the policy you actually run
The same TD residual becomes a critic

cap.1: SARSA is the careful learner that counts on its own clumsiness. Judging a policy by how it will really behave matters most when mistakes are costly.
cap.2: On-policy versus off-policy is the split between SARSA and Q-learning. SARSA's one-step TD residual comes back as the critic's loss in actor-critic.
cap.3: When you evaluate an agent, say which policy you mean: the one it runs, exploration included, or the greedy one. Getting that wrong misjudges how safe it is, a core question in steering AI.

readouts.f: (-13 - 11*(e/4)*P) > (-17 - (e/4)*P) ? 'the edge (what Q-learning learns)' : 'the detour (what SARSA learns)'

caption.1: Slide the stumble rate. With no stumbling the edge route is shorter. At about one stumble in sixty the detour starts winning, and ARENA uses one in ten.
caption.2: Toy expected returns for each route under ε-greedy. The edge route makes 11 moves where one random action drops you off; the detour makes 1. SARSA's values price this in; Q-learning's max target leaves it out.
caption.3: Toy: each risky move has chance ε/4 of the fatal action at cost P; path lengths 13 and 17; harmless random moves ignored. Break-even ε = 1.6/P. At ε = 0.1, P = 100 the detour wins easily.

where_else: Q-learning, its off-policy sibling: the same update with a max in place of the next action
Actor-critic, where the same one-step TD residual becomes the critic's loss
Any evaluation of an agent that must say whether it means the policy as run or the greedy one

hamming.what: An RL update that nudges Q(s, a) towards the reward plus the value of the action the agent actually takes next.
hamming.when: When you learn values from your own experience and will still be exploring, or making mistakes, when it counts.
hamming.why: It learns the value of the policy it actually runs, so it prices in its own exploration and learns cautious routes where mistakes are costly.

object.title: The dread map
object.subtitle: CliffWalking's 4 × 12 grid: tower height is how badly the learner expects things to go from each square.

cap.1: The cliff walk's grid. The row of stubs is the cliff. Tower height is how badly SARSA expects things to go from each square.
cap.2: A stylised cost-to-go map: taller means a worse expected future from that square, under SARSA with ε = 0.1.
cap.3: Height ≈ −V_π(s): steps remaining plus, for SARSA, the expected cliff penalty from ε-random moves.

cap.1: The row beside the cliff towers over its neighbours. SARSA remembers that a stumble there can be fatal, so it keeps its distance.
cap.2: Edge-adjacent squares carry the expected −100 from random 'down' moves, so SARSA's greedy route avoids them.
cap.3: Q_π of edge-adjacent states includes P(random down)·(−100) ≈ (ε/4)·(−100) per visit, enough to flip the argmax.

cap.1: Switch to Q-learning and the dread beside the cliff vanishes. It rates each square by its best next step, so the edge looks perfectly safe.
cap.2: Q-learning's max target ignores its own exploration, so the edge row looks as good as any other.
cap.3: Off-policy targets estimate Q*, which excludes behaviour-policy noise; the greedy path is the edge.

cap.1: SARSA with no stumbling: the dread vanishes here too. When nobody stumbles, the step you take next is the best one.
cap.2: At ε = 0 the action actually taken is the greedy one, so the SARSA and Q-learning targets coincide.
cap.3: As ε → 0 the ε-greedy π approaches greedy and Q_π approaches Q*: the two algorithms meet.

cap.1: Stumble more and the dread grows: the more random the walk, the more SARSA wants to stay away from the edge.
cap.2: Higher ε means a higher chance of a fatal random move, so SARSA's values push its route further from the edge.
cap.3: The priced-in penalty scales with ε; SARSA's learned route depends on its own exploration rate.

predict.q: With ε = 0.1 on CliffWalking, which learner ends up hugging the cliff edge?
predict.why: Q-learning's max target ignores its own random steps, so the edge looks safe. SARSA prices them in.

predict.q: Rolled out greedily after training, which route scores better?
predict.why: With exploration switched off nobody stumbles, so the shorter edge path wins.

predict.q: Your SARSA agent behaves exactly like Q-learning. Most likely bug?

options.t: The a′ in the update isn't the action actually taken next
The learning rate is too high

predict.why: An argmax, or a re-sampled action, removes the random branch and turns SARSA into Q-learning.

object.where: Any learner judged by the policy it actually runs: on-policy methods, actor-critic's critic, safe exploration.
